name: evidence_types
description: What can support a claim and how it is presented — testimony, documents, statistics and their framing, examples, authorities, comparisons, study designs, case selection, and the hierarchy of sources — with the misuse risk attached to each.

testimonial_evidence.name: eyewitness testimony
testimonial_evidence.definition: A first-hand account of an observed event by someone present at it.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Confidence tracks accuracy poorly; memory is reconstructive and vulnerable to suggestion between the event and the account.
testimonial_evidence.example: A bystander describes the sequence of the collision.

testimonial_evidence.name: expert testimony
testimonial_evidence.definition: An opinion offered by someone qualified by training or experience to interpret evidence a lay audience cannot.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Check that the opinion falls inside the witness's actual specialty and that the methods are accepted in the field, not invented for the case.

testimonial_evidence.name: lay opinion
testimonial_evidence.definition: An ordinary observer's inference from what they perceived — speed, mood, intoxication — rather than raw description.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Legitimate only for judgments people make routinely; it smuggles in interpretation.

testimonial_evidence.name: hearsay
testimonial_evidence.definition: A report of what someone else said, offered to establish that what they said was true.
testimonial_evidence.caution: The original speaker cannot be questioned; each retelling loses qualification and gains confidence.

testimonial_evidence.name: double hearsay
testimonial_evidence.definition: A report of a report — two or more links between the assertion and anyone who observed anything.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Error compounds at every link; trace the chain to its first link or drop the claim.

testimonial_evidence.name: statement against interest
testimonial_evidence.definition: An assertion that damages the speaker's own position, which is therefore less likely to be self-serving invention.
testimonial_evidence.example: A firm's own filing concedes the defect rate.

testimonial_evidence.name: excited utterance
testimonial_evidence.definition: A statement made under the immediate stress of an event, before reflection could shape it.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Spontaneity buys sincerity, not accuracy — stress degrades perception.

testimonial_evidence.name: present sense impression
testimonial_evidence.definition: A description made while perceiving the event or immediately after, minimizing memory decay.
testimonial_evidence.example: A dispatcher's log entry written as the call came in.

testimonial_evidence.name: dying declaration
testimonial_evidence.definition: A statement about the cause of one's own impending death, traditionally admitted despite hearsay rules.
testimonial_evidence.caution: A legal category, not an epistemic guarantee.

testimonial_evidence.name: party admission
testimonial_evidence.definition: A statement by a party to a dispute, used against them by their opponent.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Context of the admission matters: negotiation talk, hypotheticals, and apologies are routinely misread as concessions of fact.

testimonial_evidence.name: deposition testimony
testimonial_evidence.definition: Sworn out-of-court testimony taken under questioning by opposing counsel and transcribed verbatim.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Excerpting a deposition changes it; the surrounding questions usually carry the qualification.

testimonial_evidence.name: sworn affidavit
testimonial_evidence.definition: A written statement made under oath or penalty of perjury, without cross-examination.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Untested by adversarial questioning; often drafted by the party's lawyer and signed.

testimonial_evidence.name: on-the-record source
testimonial_evidence.definition: A named source who accepts attribution for what they say.
testimonial_evidence.example: The commissioner, by name, confirming the timeline.

testimonial_evidence.name: background source
testimonial_evidence.definition: A source whose information may be used with an agreed non-identifying description.
testimonial_evidence.caution: The description ('a person familiar with the matter') hides both the source's access and their stake.

testimonial_evidence.name: anonymous source
testimonial_evidence.definition: A source whose identity is withheld entirely, typically because disclosure carries risk.
testimonial_evidence.caution: The reader cannot assess motive or access; requires corroboration and an explicit reason for the anonymity.

testimonial_evidence.name: whistleblower account
testimonial_evidence.definition: An insider's disclosure of wrongdoing, usually against their own interest and with documentary support.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Insider access is real but partial; the vantage point shapes what is visible.

testimonial_evidence.name: oral history
testimonial_evidence.definition: A recorded long-form recollection collected as a historical source in its own right.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Excellent for meaning, texture, and lived experience; weak for dates, quantities, and sequence.

testimonial_evidence.name: contemporaneous notes
testimonial_evidence.definition: Notes written at or near the time of the events they describe.
testimonial_evidence.example: A field notebook dated the day of the inspection.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Establish when they were written; notes 'reconstructed later' are memory, not record.

testimonial_evidence.name: self-report survey response
testimonial_evidence.definition: A subject's own account of their behavior, attitudes, or history, collected instrumentally.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Subject to social desirability, recall error, and question wording; behaviors are systematically over- or under-reported by category.

testimonial_evidence.name: character and reputation evidence
testimonial_evidence.definition: Testimony about how a person is regarded in a community, offered to support or undercut credibility.
testimonial_evidence.caution: Rarely bears on a specific act; strongly prejudicial relative to its probative value.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: primary document
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A record produced by a participant in or witness to the events, without an intervening interpreter.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.example: The original contract, the minutes taken at the meeting.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: business record
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A document created in the regular course of an organization's operations, at or near the time of the transaction.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Regularity is the basis of its reliability; a record created for the dispute is not one.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: public record
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A document filed with or produced by a government body and available for inspection.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.example: Property deeds, licensing registers, inspection reports.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: court filing
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A pleading, motion, exhibit, or order entered on a case docket.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Allegations in a complaint are claims, not findings; cite the ruling, not the pleading, for what was decided.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: hearing transcript
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A verbatim record of spoken proceedings, produced by a certified reporter or an audited machine pass.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Transcripts drop tone and cross-talk; check the certification and the errata sheet.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: regulatory filing
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A disclosure a regulated entity is legally required to submit, often under penalty for misstatement.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: audited financial statement
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Financial accounts examined by an independent auditor against a reporting standard.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: An audit opinion covers material misstatement under a standard, not economic reality; read the opinion type and the notes.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: internal memorandum
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A document written for internal circulation, revealing what an organization believed or intended at the time.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Internal documents are often drafts or advocacy; distinguish a proposal from a decision.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: correspondence
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Letters, emails, or messages between identified parties, evidencing knowledge, timing, and intent.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Threads are quoted out of order routinely; check headers, timestamps, and who was actually on the message.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: leaked document
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: An internal record disclosed without the holder's authorization.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Authenticate independently and consider selection: the leaker chose which documents you see.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: freedom-of-information release
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Records disclosed by a public body in response to a statutory request, often with redactions.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Redaction and exemption patterns shape the picture; note what was withheld and under which exemption.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: administrative dataset
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Records generated by an operating system of administration — tax, benefits, registration — repurposed as data.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Definitions follow administrative need, change without notice, and count only what the system touches.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: system log
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Machine-generated event records with timestamps, produced automatically rather than composed.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Clock drift, timezone handling, and retention windows determine what a log can prove.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: file metadata
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Embedded creation, modification, authorship, and device fields attached to a digital artifact.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Trivially editable and routinely rewritten by ordinary copying and export.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: photographic evidence
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A still image offered as a record of an appearance, condition, or event.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Framing, lens, and moment are choices; provenance and unedited originals matter more than the image.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: video footage
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A moving-image record, often with continuous timing that fixes sequence and duration.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Angle, frame rate, and edit points change perceived causation; establish the full unedited clip.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: audio recording
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A captured record of speech or sound, preserving wording and tone.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Ambiguous audio is heard as whatever a caption suggests; provide the transcript and the raw file.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: physical trace evidence
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Material residue — marks, fragments, wear patterns — interpreted through a forensic discipline.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Interpretive strength varies enormously across disciplines; several long-accepted comparison methods lack validated error rates.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: chain of custody record
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: Documentation of every transfer and storage condition of an item of evidence from collection to analysis.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: A gap in custody does not prove tampering but removes the basis for excluding it.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: archival collection
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: An organized body of retained records with a finding aid describing provenance and arrangement.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Archives preserve what someone chose to keep; the shape of the collection is itself evidence about the keeper.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: map or survey record
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A spatial record of boundaries, features, or measurements made to a stated standard.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Projection, datum, and survey date determine what the lines mean.

documentary_and_physical_evidence.name: instrument reading
documentary_and_physical_evidence.definition: A measurement produced by a calibrated device rather than by human judgment.
documentary_and_physical_evidence.caution: Calibration date, detection limit, and units are part of the evidence; a reading without them is a number.

statistical_forms.name: point estimate
statistical_forms.definition: A single value offered as the best estimate of a quantity in the population.
statistical_forms.caution: Meaningless without an interval; a point estimate presented alone implies precision it does not have.

statistical_forms.name: confidence interval
statistical_forms.definition: A range constructed so that, over repeated sampling, a stated proportion of such intervals would contain the true value.
statistical_forms.caution: It is not the probability that the parameter lies in this interval; and it covers sampling error only, not bias.

statistical_forms.name: margin of error
statistical_forms.definition: Half-width of the confidence interval for a survey estimate, typically at 95%.
statistical_forms.caution: Applies to the full sample; subgroup margins are much wider, and non-response bias is not included.

statistical_forms.name: standard error
statistical_forms.definition: The standard deviation of an estimate's sampling distribution — how much the estimate would move across samples.
statistical_forms.caution: Often confused with the standard deviation of the data, which describes spread, not estimate precision.

statistical_forms.name: p-value
statistical_forms.definition: The probability of data at least as extreme as observed, if the null hypothesis were true.
statistical_forms.caution: Not the probability the hypothesis is true, not a measure of effect size, and not a threshold of importance.

statistical_forms.name: effect size
statistical_forms.definition: A standardized magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size.
statistical_forms.example: Cohen's d, Hedges' g, correlation r.
statistical_forms.caution: Standardized units hide practical meaning; translate back into the raw scale for the reader.

statistical_forms.name: absolute risk difference
statistical_forms.definition: The arithmetic difference in event rates between two groups.
statistical_forms.caution: The honest headline number, and the one most often omitted in favor of relative measures.

statistical_forms.name: relative risk
statistical_forms.definition: The ratio of the event rate in the exposed group to the rate in the unexposed.
statistical_forms.caution: A large ratio on a tiny base rate is a small change in the world.

statistical_forms.name: odds ratio
statistical_forms.definition: The ratio of the odds of an outcome in one group to the odds in another.
statistical_forms.caution: Approximates relative risk only for rare outcomes; for common outcomes it exaggerates.

statistical_forms.name: number needed to treat
statistical_forms.definition: How many people must receive an intervention for one additional good outcome to occur.
statistical_forms.example: An NNT of 90 means 89 of 90 treated see no benefit from this outcome.

statistical_forms.name: hazard ratio
statistical_forms.definition: The ratio of instantaneous event rates between groups over follow-up time.
statistical_forms.caution: Assumes the ratio is constant over time; check the survival curves for crossings.

statistical_forms.name: correlation coefficient
statistical_forms.definition: A standardized measure of linear association between two variables, from -1 to 1.
statistical_forms.caution: Blind to non-linear relationships, driven by outliers, and unrelated to causation or to slope.

statistical_forms.name: regression coefficient
statistical_forms.definition: The estimated change in the outcome per unit change in a predictor, holding other model terms fixed.
statistical_forms.caution: 'Holding fixed' is a property of the model, not of the world; controls can also be colliders.

statistical_forms.name: coefficient of determination
statistical_forms.definition: The share of variance in the outcome accounted for by the model.
statistical_forms.caution: High R-squared can accompany a useless model, and low R-squared a real effect.

statistical_forms.name: standard deviation
statistical_forms.definition: A summary of how far values typically fall from the mean.
statistical_forms.caution: Interpretable as a rule of thumb only for roughly symmetric distributions.

statistical_forms.name: interquartile range
statistical_forms.definition: The spread of the middle half of the data, from the 25th to the 75th percentile.
statistical_forms.caution: A good companion to the median; still says nothing about extremes.

statistical_forms.name: rate
statistical_forms.definition: A count normalized by exposure — population, person-years, vehicle-miles.
statistical_forms.caution: The denominator is the argument; state it explicitly every time.

statistical_forms.name: prevalence
statistical_forms.definition: The share of a population with a condition at a point in time.
statistical_forms.caution: Reflects both how often the condition arises and how long it lasts.

statistical_forms.name: incidence
statistical_forms.definition: The rate of new cases arising in a population over a period.
statistical_forms.caution: Routinely confused with prevalence; changes in one can move the other in the opposite direction.

statistical_forms.name: sensitivity and specificity
statistical_forms.definition: A test's true-positive rate among those with the condition and true-negative rate among those without.
statistical_forms.caution: Both are properties of the test, not answers to the reader's question, which needs prevalence too.

statistical_forms.name: positive predictive value
statistical_forms.definition: The probability that a positive result is a true positive, given the population's base rate.
statistical_forms.caution: Falls sharply as prevalence falls, which is why screening rare conditions produces mostly false alarms.

statistical_forms.name: likelihood ratio
statistical_forms.definition: How much more likely a finding is under one hypothesis than another — the multiplier on prior odds.
statistical_forms.example: A likelihood ratio of 10 shifts odds by an order of magnitude.

statistical_forms.name: posterior probability
statistical_forms.definition: The probability of a hypothesis after updating a stated prior with the evidence.
statistical_forms.caution: Requires the prior to be stated and defended; hidden priors do the work in most Bayesian rhetoric.

statistical_forms.name: statistical power
statistical_forms.definition: The probability a study would detect an effect of a stated size if it exists.
statistical_forms.caution: Underpowered null results are uninformative; power calculated after the fact from the observed effect is meaningless.

statistical_forms.name: pooled effect estimate
statistical_forms.definition: A weighted combination of results across studies in a meta-analysis.
statistical_forms.caution: Pooling incompatible designs and populations produces a precise number describing nothing.

statistical_forms.name: heterogeneity statistic
statistical_forms.definition: A measure of how much variation across pooled studies exceeds chance.
statistical_forms.example: High I-squared says the studies are estimating different things.

statistical_forms.name: prediction interval
statistical_forms.definition: A range expected to contain a future individual observation, not just the mean.
statistical_forms.caution: Always wider than a confidence interval; the one readers actually want when asking 'what will happen to me'.

statistical_forms.name: index number
statistical_forms.definition: A composite series rescaled to a base period to summarize movement in a bundle.
statistical_forms.caution: Weights and basket composition determine the story; a reweighted index is a different index.

statistical_forms.name: elasticity
statistical_forms.definition: The percentage change in one quantity per percentage change in another.
statistical_forms.caution: Estimated locally; it does not survive extrapolation to large changes.

statistical_forms.name: compound growth rate
statistical_forms.definition: The constant rate that would take a series from its start value to its end value over the period.
statistical_forms.caution: Endpoint-sensitive: shifting the start year by one can reverse the impression.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: per-capita framing
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Expressing a count relative to population so that units of different size can be compared.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: The relevant denominator is not always population — exposure, vehicle-miles, or patient-days may be the right base.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: absolute-and-relative pairing
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Reporting the change both as a ratio and in absolute terms so neither impression stands alone.
statistics_presentation_modes.example: Risk rose 50% — from 2 in 10,000 to 3 in 10,000.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: natural frequencies
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Expressing conditional probabilities as counts within a stated reference group.
statistics_presentation_modes.example: Of 1,000 tested, 10 have the condition; 9 test positive; 99 healthy people also test positive.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: The single most effective repair for base-rate confusion in lay and expert readers alike.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: denominator disclosure
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Naming the population, time window, and inclusion rule behind every rate in the text.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Where the denominator is unstated, assume it was chosen.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: inflation adjustment
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Converting nominal amounts to constant currency of a stated year.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Name the index and base year; different deflators give materially different histories.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: seasonal adjustment
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Removing recurring within-year patterns so that underlying movement is visible.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Adjusted series get revised; month-to-month changes in adjusted data are often smaller than the revision.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: age standardization
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Reweighting rates to a common age structure so populations of different ages can be compared.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: The standard population chosen changes the numbers; state it.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: indexed-to-baseline presentation
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Rescaling several series to 100 at a common date to compare growth rather than level.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Choice of base date determines the visual ranking entirely.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: logarithmic scale
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Plotting on a log axis so that equal vertical distances represent equal proportional change.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Honest for growth processes and misread by most general readers; label it loudly.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: zero-baseline bar chart
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Anchoring bar length at zero so that visual length is proportional to value.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: The convention exists because truncated bars misstate ratios; line charts of levels may legitimately omit zero.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: rolling average
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Smoothing a noisy series by averaging over a moving window.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Suppresses turning points and lags them by roughly half the window.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: cumulative versus periodic framing
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Choosing between running totals and per-period counts, which tell different stories about the same data.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Cumulative curves can only rise, which makes any slowdown look like continued growth.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: share-of-total framing
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Presenting components as percentages of a whole rather than as levels.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: A share can fall while the level rises; say which one moved.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: rank versus level presentation
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Reporting position in a league table instead of the underlying magnitude.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Ranks hide how close the field is; a three-place drop may be a rounding error.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: disaggregation by subgroup
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Splitting an aggregate into components to show whether the average describes anyone.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Post-hoc subgroup splitting multiplies false positives; prespecify or label as exploratory.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: uncertainty visualization
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Showing error bars, bands, or fan charts so that the estimate's precision is visible with the estimate.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: State what the band represents — standard error, 95% interval, prediction interval — since they differ by a factor of two or more.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: sensitivity analysis
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Reporting how the conclusion changes under alternative defensible assumptions.
statistics_presentation_modes.example: The result holds under all three discount rates.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: fermi estimate
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: An order-of-magnitude calculation from decomposable, checkable assumptions.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Excellent for sanity-checking a claim; never a substitute for measurement when measurement exists.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: familiar-reference-class framing
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Expressing a risk or quantity in a unit the reader already calibrates against.
statistics_presentation_modes.example: The same risk as driving 200 miles.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: significant-figure discipline
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Rounding reported numbers to the precision the estimate actually supports.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Extra decimals are a claim about measurement quality; readers hear them as one.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: one-in-N phrasing
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Expressing a small probability as a count within a concrete population.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Comparisons between one-in-N figures with different N are read badly; keep the reference constant.

statistics_presentation_modes.name: small multiples
statistics_presentation_modes.definition: Repeating one chart form across categories on a shared scale so comparison is direct.
statistics_presentation_modes.caution: Only works if the scale is genuinely shared.

example_types.name: representative case
example_types.definition: An instance chosen because it is typical of the class the claim is about.
example_types.caution: Typicality must be argued from the distribution, not asserted.

example_types.name: extreme case
example_types.definition: An instance at the far end of the relevant scale, used to expose a mechanism at maximum visibility.
example_types.caution: Reveals what is possible, not what is usual.

example_types.name: counterexample
example_types.definition: A single instance that falls under a general claim and violates it.
example_types.example: One documented case is enough against 'never'.

example_types.name: hard case
example_types.definition: An instance near the boundary, where the rule under discussion gives an uncomfortable answer.
example_types.caution: Hard cases test a rule's limits; they are poor material for building one.

example_types.name: paradigm case
example_types.definition: The uncontested central instance of a concept, used to anchor its meaning.
example_types.example: If this is not fraud, the word has no application.

example_types.name: borderline case
example_types.definition: An instance whose classification is genuinely unsettled, used to expose vagueness.
example_types.caution: Useful for definition work; misleading as evidence about the central cases.

example_types.name: limiting case
example_types.definition: The degenerate instance where a parameter goes to zero or infinity, testing whether a claim still behaves.
example_types.example: What does the formula say for a population of one?

example_types.name: thought experiment
example_types.definition: An imagined, fully specified scenario constructed to isolate a variable that reality confounds.
example_types.caution: Yields conceptual conclusions only; intuitions about vivid hypotheticals are unstable.

example_types.name: hypothetical
example_types.definition: An invented but realistic scenario used to test how a rule or principle would apply.
example_types.caution: Whoever writes the facts wins the hypothetical; invite the other side to vary them.

example_types.name: intuition pump
example_types.definition: A narrative device engineered so a particular intuition emerges, with knobs that can be turned to test its robustness.
example_types.caution: Turn the knobs; if the intuition flips on an irrelevant detail, it was not tracking the principle.

example_types.name: reductio example
example_types.definition: A case constructed so that applying the opponent's principle to it yields an unacceptable result.
example_types.caution: Only bites if the case really falls under the principle as stated.

example_types.name: anecdote
example_types.definition: A single real incident recounted for its illustrative or emotional force.
example_types.caution: Carries no inferential weight about frequency; readers over-generalize from it anyway, so mark its status.

example_types.name: vignette
example_types.definition: A short compressed scene, real or constructed, that renders an abstraction concrete.
example_types.example: Two paragraphs following one claim through the appeals process.

example_types.name: composite case
example_types.definition: A single narrative assembled from features of several real cases.
example_types.caution: Must be disclosed as composite; presented as one person's story it is fabrication.

example_types.name: worked example
example_types.definition: A calculation or procedure carried through step by step with real numbers.
example_types.example: Running the same claim through the formula with the reported figures.

example_types.name: negative example
example_types.definition: An instance of what the concept is not, used to sharpen its boundary by contrast.
example_types.example: This is delegation; that is abdication.

example_types.name: existence proof
example_types.definition: A single demonstrated instance establishing that something is possible.
example_types.caution: Establishes possibility only — never frequency, cost, or scalability.

example_types.name: minimal pair
example_types.definition: Two cases identical except in the one feature at issue, isolating that feature's effect.
example_types.example: The same application under two names.

example_types.name: stylized fact
example_types.definition: A broad empirical regularity, deliberately simplified, that a theory is expected to reproduce.
example_types.caution: Simplification hides exceptions; check that the regularity survives at the level of your claim.

example_types.name: running example
example_types.definition: One case carried through an entire argument, taking on new aspects at each stage.
example_types.caution: Efficient and memorable, but the reader may generalize the whole argument from the one case.

example_types.name: cautionary case
example_types.definition: A documented failure presented to establish that a risk is realized in practice, not just in principle.
example_types.caution: Selection matters: one disaster does not establish a rate.

example_types.name: demonstration
example_types.definition: An in-text performance of the phenomenon rather than a description of it.
example_types.example: A paragraph written in the style it is criticizing.

authority_types.name: subject-matter expert
authority_types.definition: A person with deep, current, domain-specific training whose judgment is credentialed by peers.
authority_types.caution: Expertise is narrow; a leading figure one subfield over is a lay reader on your question.

authority_types.name: experienced practitioner
authority_types.definition: Someone whose authority comes from repeated hands-on engagement rather than formal study.
authority_types.caution: Strong on tacit knowledge and failure modes, weak on frequencies and on cases they never see.

authority_types.name: institutional authority
authority_types.definition: An organization whose standing, procedures, and accountability underwrite a claim.
authority_types.caution: Institutional endorsement is a procedural guarantee, not an evidentiary one.

authority_types.name: regulatory body
authority_types.definition: A public agency empowered to set and enforce binding requirements in a domain.
authority_types.caution: Its determinations reflect legal mandate and evidentiary standard, which may differ from scientific consensus.

authority_types.name: standards organization
authority_types.definition: A body that publishes consensus technical standards through a documented process.

authority_types.name: adjudicative authority
authority_types.definition: A court or tribunal whose findings of fact are made under procedural rules and a stated standard of proof.
authority_types.caution: A verdict is a legal resolution under a burden of proof, not a scientific finding.

authority_types.name: consensus statement
authority_types.definition: A position developed by a convened panel of specialists reviewing evidence to a stated method.
authority_types.caution: Check who convened the panel, who sat on it, and how dissent was recorded.

authority_types.name: systematic review body
authority_types.definition: An organization whose function is to appraise and synthesize evidence to a published protocol.

authority_types.name: professional guideline
authority_types.definition: A recommendation issued by a professional body to guide practice, usually with graded evidence levels.
authority_types.caution: Read the grade attached to each recommendation; strong recommendations often rest on weak evidence.

authority_types.name: official statistics agency
authority_types.definition: A national or supranational body producing statistics under methodological and independence standards.
authority_types.caution: Definitions and series breaks are documented in the methodology notes and ignored in most citations.

authority_types.name: reference work
authority_types.definition: A curated compilation — dictionary, handbook, standard treatise — whose authority is editorial and cumulative.
authority_types.caution: Lags the field by years; use it for settled meaning, not for the frontier.

authority_types.name: textbook authority
authority_types.definition: A teaching text presenting the consolidated view of a field to newcomers.
authority_types.caution: Simplifies deliberately; a textbook claim is a summary of a literature, not a citation to it.

authority_types.name: principal investigator
authority_types.definition: The researcher who designed and ran the study, able to speak to decisions not visible in the paper.
authority_types.caution: Also the party most invested in the interpretation.

authority_types.name: journalist of record
authority_types.definition: A reporter with a sustained beat, institutional editing, and correction practice.
authority_types.caution: Reporting is a secondary source; follow it to its documents.

authority_types.name: insider with access
authority_types.definition: A source whose authority is positional — they were in the room — rather than expert.
authority_types.caution: Access is not perspective; a participant's view of a system is partial by construction.

authority_types.name: forecaster with a track record
authority_types.definition: A person or market whose predictive authority rests on scored, public, out-of-sample performance.
authority_types.caution: Demand the full record, including resolved misses; selective retrospectives are the norm.

authority_types.name: canonical text
authority_types.definition: A foundational work treated as authoritative within a tradition.
authority_types.caution: Its authority is interpretive and internal to the tradition; citing it settles usage, not fact.

comparison_devices.name: analogy
comparison_devices.definition: Evidential sense: transferring understanding from a familiar case to an unfamiliar one on the basis of shared relevant structure, offered in support of a claim. Distinct from the figure, which is judged by aptness rather than by how far the structures actually correspond.
comparison_devices.caution: Every analogy has a breaking point; name it before a critic does.

comparison_devices.name: disanalogy
comparison_devices.definition: Explicitly marking where a comparison stops holding, to bound what it licenses.
comparison_devices.example: Like a mortgage, except that the collateral can vanish.

comparison_devices.name: benchmark comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Measuring a case against an agreed reference standard.
comparison_devices.caution: The benchmark encodes a set of values; who chose it, and what does it reward?

comparison_devices.name: before-and-after comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing measurements from the same unit across an intervention.
comparison_devices.caution: Without a control, this confounds the intervention with every trend and shock in the same period.

comparison_devices.name: control-group comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing treated units to comparable untreated units over the same period.
comparison_devices.caution: Comparability is the whole argument; state how it was achieved.

comparison_devices.name: counterfactual comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing what happened to a constructed estimate of what would have happened otherwise.
comparison_devices.caution: Make the counterfactual explicit and falsifiable, or it is a preference in the form of a number.

comparison_devices.name: cross-national comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing outcomes across countries to isolate the effect of institutions or policy.
comparison_devices.caution: Definitions, measurement systems, and compositions differ; harmonization is usually assumed rather than done.

comparison_devices.name: peer-group comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing a unit to a defined set of similar units rather than to the whole population.
comparison_devices.caution: Peer-group definition determines the result; peer sets are frequently drawn to flatter.

comparison_devices.name: historical parallel
comparison_devices.definition: Setting a present case beside a past one to import its lessons.
comparison_devices.caution: The lesson depends on which features are held to matter; base rates of successful historical analogy are poor.

comparison_devices.name: scale comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Rendering a magnitude comprehensible by equating it to a familiar physical or budgetary quantity.
comparison_devices.example: An area the size of a mid-sized state.
comparison_devices.caution: Familiar referents distort in their own way; a state's area is not well known either.

comparison_devices.name: unit conversion to human terms
comparison_devices.definition: Recasting an aggregate into per-person, per-day, or per-household units.
comparison_devices.example: The program costs about the price of a coffee per taxpayer per month.
comparison_devices.caution: The device systematically shrinks large sums; use it symmetrically for costs and benefits.

comparison_devices.name: ratio comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Expressing one quantity as a multiple of another to make relative size vivid.
comparison_devices.caution: Ratios of small numbers are unstable; report the components.

comparison_devices.name: chance-level baseline
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing performance to what random behavior would achieve.
comparison_devices.example: Sixty percent accuracy on a two-way task is ten points above guessing.

comparison_devices.name: best-in-class comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Measuring against the leading performer to show the size of the achievable gap.
comparison_devices.caution: The frontier case may be unrepresentative or unreachable for structural reasons.

comparison_devices.name: worst-case comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Setting a case against the plausible floor to establish that current conditions are not the bottom.
comparison_devices.caution: Easily becomes relative privation — 'it could be worse' is not a defense.

comparison_devices.name: cost-benefit comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Placing consequences of an action on a common scale to compare totals.
comparison_devices.caution: Monetization decisions and discount rates carry the conclusion; expose them.

comparison_devices.name: opportunity-cost comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing an option not to nothing but to the best displaced alternative.
comparison_devices.caution: The alternative must be genuinely available with the same resources.

comparison_devices.name: side-by-side matrix
comparison_devices.definition: A table comparing options along shared, stated criteria.
comparison_devices.caution: Criterion selection and row order do the persuading; a matrix looks neutral and rarely is.

comparison_devices.name: trend comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing rates of change rather than levels between series.
comparison_devices.caution: Different starting points make growth rates non-comparable; show the levels too.

comparison_devices.name: order-of-magnitude comparison
comparison_devices.definition: Comparing quantities by powers of ten rather than exact values, to establish which dominates.
comparison_devices.example: One is a rounding error on the other.

case_selection_strategies.name: typical case selection
case_selection_strategies.definition: Choosing a case that sits at the center of the distribution to explore the usual mechanism.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Good for mechanism, weak for range.

case_selection_strategies.name: deviant case selection
case_selection_strategies.definition: Choosing a case the existing theory fails to explain, to expose an omitted variable.
case_selection_strategies.example: The one district where the reform reduced enrollment.

case_selection_strategies.name: crucial case selection
case_selection_strategies.definition: Choosing a case where a theory's prediction is most clearly at stake, so the result is maximally informative.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Crucial-case status must be argued from the theory before the result is known.

case_selection_strategies.name: least-likely case
case_selection_strategies.definition: Confirming a theory in a case where conditions were least favorable to it, which strengthens the inference.
case_selection_strategies.example: If it works here, it should work anywhere.

case_selection_strategies.name: most-likely case
case_selection_strategies.definition: Testing a theory where conditions maximally favor it, so failure is strongly disconfirming.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Success in a most-likely case establishes very little.

case_selection_strategies.name: most-similar systems design
case_selection_strategies.definition: Comparing cases alike in most respects but differing in the outcome, to isolate the difference that matters.
case_selection_strategies.caution: 'Alike in most respects' is a claim to defend with evidence, not a stipulation.

case_selection_strategies.name: most-different systems design
case_selection_strategies.definition: Comparing cases that differ in most respects yet share the outcome, to find a common factor.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Shared factors are easy to find post hoc; prespecify candidates.

case_selection_strategies.name: paired comparison
case_selection_strategies.definition: Analyzing two matched cases in depth against each other rather than against a population.
case_selection_strategies.example: Two neighboring towns that adopted opposite policies.

case_selection_strategies.name: pathway case
case_selection_strategies.definition: Selecting a case where the causal mechanism should be observable in operation, to trace it directly.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Mechanism visibility, not representativeness, is the criterion; do not generalize frequencies from it.

case_selection_strategies.name: influential case
case_selection_strategies.definition: Examining the case that drives an aggregate result, to test whether the finding is an artifact of one observation.
case_selection_strategies.example: Dropping the largest state reverses the correlation.

case_selection_strategies.name: process tracing
case_selection_strategies.definition: Following the sequence of events within a case to test whether the hypothesized mechanism actually operated.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Requires evidence at each link; a plausible narrative that fits the outcome is not a trace.

case_selection_strategies.name: negative case analysis
case_selection_strategies.definition: Deliberately seeking cases that do not fit the emerging account and revising until they do or are explained.
case_selection_strategies.caution: The default without it is confirmation by accumulation.

case_selection_strategies.name: disconfirming case search
case_selection_strategies.definition: Actively hunting for the observation that would falsify the claim before publishing it.
case_selection_strategies.example: Looking for the counterexample yourself so a reviewer does not have to.

case_selection_strategies.name: purposive sampling
case_selection_strategies.definition: Selecting cases deliberately for their informational value against stated criteria.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Legitimate for qualitative inference, illegitimate for estimating proportions.

case_selection_strategies.name: theoretical saturation sampling
case_selection_strategies.definition: Continuing to add cases until new ones stop yielding new categories.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Saturation is a judgment; report how it was assessed.

case_selection_strategies.name: stratified sampling
case_selection_strategies.definition: Dividing the population into strata and sampling within each to guarantee coverage.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Strata must be weighted back when producing population estimates.

case_selection_strategies.name: random case selection
case_selection_strategies.definition: Selecting cases by chance from a defined frame to eliminate selection on unobservables.
case_selection_strategies.caution: With small numbers of cases, random selection can still produce an unrepresentative set.

case_selection_strategies.name: snowball sampling
case_selection_strategies.definition: Recruiting further cases through referrals from existing ones, used for hidden populations.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Samples network clusters, not populations; well-connected members are over-represented.

case_selection_strategies.name: convenience sampling
case_selection_strategies.definition: Selecting whatever cases are accessible.
case_selection_strategies.caution: The default and the weakest; state it plainly rather than describing the sample as if it were drawn.

case_selection_strategies.name: longitudinal single case
case_selection_strategies.definition: Following one case over time so it serves as its own comparison.
case_selection_strategies.caution: Controls stable case features, not period effects.

study_designs.name: randomized controlled trial
study_designs.definition: Units are assigned to conditions by chance, so treatment is independent of both observed and unobserved characteristics.
study_designs.caution: Internal validity is bought with narrow populations, short horizons, and consent-based samples.

study_designs.name: cluster randomized trial
study_designs.definition: Randomization at the group level — school, clinic, village — when the intervention operates on groups.
study_designs.caution: Effective sample size is the number of clusters, not participants; analyses that ignore this overstate precision.

study_designs.name: crossover trial
study_designs.definition: Each unit receives both conditions in a randomized order and serves as its own control.
study_designs.caution: Requires the effect to wash out between periods; carryover invalidates the design.

study_designs.name: stepped-wedge trial
study_designs.definition: All units eventually receive the intervention, with the timing of rollout randomized.
study_designs.caution: Confounded with time trends unless the analysis models them.

study_designs.name: prospective cohort study
study_designs.definition: A defined group is followed forward in time and outcomes are recorded as they occur.
study_designs.caution: Exposure is not assigned; confounding by indication is the standing threat.

study_designs.name: retrospective cohort study
study_designs.definition: A cohort is assembled from existing records and followed forward within them.
study_designs.caution: Limited to what the records happened to capture, and to units the records covered.

study_designs.name: case-control study
study_designs.definition: Cases with the outcome and controls without it are compared on prior exposure.
study_designs.caution: Efficient for rare outcomes; vulnerable to recall bias and to control-selection bias, and yields odds, not risks.

study_designs.name: cross-sectional survey
study_designs.definition: Exposure and outcome are measured at the same moment in a sample of a population.
study_designs.caution: Cannot establish temporal order, so it cannot distinguish cause from consequence.

study_designs.name: ecological study
study_designs.definition: Analysis at the level of groups or areas rather than individuals.
study_designs.caution: Cheap, wide, and exposed to the ecological fallacy; hypothesis-generating at best.

study_designs.name: case series
study_designs.definition: A descriptive account of several cases sharing an exposure or outcome, with no comparison group.
study_designs.caution: Detects new phenomena and signals; establishes no rate and no effect.

study_designs.name: single case report
study_designs.definition: A detailed description of one instance, published for its novelty or instructive value.
study_designs.caution: The bottom of every evidence hierarchy and the origin of many real discoveries; treat as a hypothesis.

study_designs.name: natural experiment
study_designs.definition: An external event assigns exposure in a way plausibly independent of the outcome, mimicking randomization.
study_designs.caution: The as-if-random claim needs defending with balance tests, not asserted from the narrative.

study_designs.name: difference-in-differences
study_designs.definition: Compares the change over time in a treated group to the change in an untreated group.
study_designs.caution: Rests on parallel pre-trends; show them.

study_designs.name: regression discontinuity
study_designs.definition: Exploits a threshold rule so that units just above and just below the cutoff are comparable.
study_designs.caution: Estimates a local effect at the threshold only; manipulation of the running variable breaks it.

study_designs.name: instrumental variables
study_designs.definition: Uses a variable that shifts exposure but affects the outcome only through it, to recover a causal effect.
study_designs.caution: The exclusion restriction is untestable and usually the weakest link; weak instruments are badly biased.

study_designs.name: propensity score matching
study_designs.definition: Matches treated and untreated units on estimated probability of treatment given observed covariates.
study_designs.caution: Balances what was measured; unobserved confounding is untouched.

study_designs.name: synthetic control
study_designs.definition: Builds a weighted combination of untreated units that reproduces the treated unit's pre-period path.
study_designs.caution: Requires a long, well-fitting pre-period and a donor pool free of spillovers.

study_designs.name: interrupted time series
study_designs.definition: Models a series before and after an intervention to detect a change in level or slope.
study_designs.caution: Sensitive to autocorrelation, seasonality, and anticipation effects.

study_designs.name: field experiment
study_designs.definition: A randomized intervention run in a real-world setting rather than a laboratory.
study_designs.caution: Gains external validity, loses control; attrition and non-compliance become central.

study_designs.name: laboratory experiment
study_designs.definition: A controlled setting where variables are manipulated and extraneous influences held constant.
study_designs.caution: Strong on mechanism, weak on generalization to stakes and populations outside the lab.

study_designs.name: audit study
study_designs.definition: Matched fictitious applications or inquiries differing in one attribute are sent to real decision-makers.
study_designs.caution: Measures the decision at one stage under the researcher's stimulus, not the full process.

study_designs.name: survey experiment
study_designs.definition: Randomly varying question wording, framing, or vignette content within a survey.
study_designs.caution: Measures stated response to a hypothetical, which may not track behavior.

study_designs.name: qualitative interview study
study_designs.definition: Systematic in-depth interviewing analyzed for themes, meanings, and mechanisms.
study_designs.caution: Answers 'how' and 'why' questions; cannot answer 'how many'.

study_designs.name: ethnography
study_designs.definition: Sustained immersion in a setting, producing an account of practice as participants live it.
study_designs.caution: Depth is bought with a single site and an inseparable observer.

study_designs.name: content analysis
study_designs.definition: Systematic coding of texts or media against a defined scheme, with reported inter-coder agreement.
study_designs.caution: Without a reported reliability statistic, coding is just reading.

study_designs.name: simulation model
study_designs.definition: A computational model producing outcomes from specified assumptions and parameters.
study_designs.caution: Output is an implication of the assumptions, never evidence about the world; report calibration and sensitivity.

study_designs.name: replication study
study_designs.definition: A repeat of an earlier study's procedure to test whether the result recurs.
study_designs.caution: Distinguish direct from conceptual replication; the latter can fail for uninformative reasons.

study_designs.name: preregistered study
study_designs.definition: A study whose hypotheses and analysis plan were deposited publicly before data collection.
study_designs.caution: Check the registration against the paper; deviations are common and often unreported.

source_hierarchy.name: primary source
source_hierarchy.definition: A record created by a direct participant or instrument, without interpretive mediation.
source_hierarchy.caution: Primary does not mean true; it means unmediated.

source_hierarchy.name: secondary source
source_hierarchy.definition: An account that interprets, synthesizes, or reports on primary material.
source_hierarchy.caution: Cite it for its analysis, not as a stand-in for the underlying record.

source_hierarchy.name: tertiary source
source_hierarchy.definition: A compilation of secondary sources — encyclopedias, handbooks, review directories.
source_hierarchy.caution: A navigation aid; almost never an acceptable citation for a contested claim.

source_hierarchy.name: systematic review
source_hierarchy.definition: A synthesis that specifies its search, inclusion criteria, and appraisal method in advance.
source_hierarchy.caution: Quality varies enormously; check the protocol, the search dates, and the risk-of-bias assessment.

source_hierarchy.name: meta-analysis
source_hierarchy.definition: A systematic review that statistically combines results across studies.
source_hierarchy.caution: Inherits every bias of its inputs and adds pooling assumptions of its own.

source_hierarchy.name: peer-reviewed article
source_hierarchy.definition: A paper accepted after review by referees selected for competence in the field.
source_hierarchy.caution: Peer review filters gross error, not fraud, and cannot verify data it never sees.

source_hierarchy.name: preprint
source_hierarchy.definition: A manuscript posted publicly before or during peer review.
source_hierarchy.caution: Fast and unfiltered; cite as a preprint explicitly and check for a later published version that differs.

source_hierarchy.name: working paper
source_hierarchy.definition: A research paper circulated by an institution or series ahead of journal publication.
source_hierarchy.caution: Standard currency in some fields, unreviewed in all; version numbers matter.

source_hierarchy.name: conference paper
source_hierarchy.definition: A paper accepted for a conference, with review standards ranging from full to abstract-only.
source_hierarchy.caution: State which; in some fields conference proceedings are the strongest venue, in others the weakest.

source_hierarchy.name: dissertation
source_hierarchy.definition: An extended supervised research work examined by a committee.
source_hierarchy.caution: Often the most thorough treatment of a narrow topic and the least read; verify whether findings were later published or abandoned.

source_hierarchy.name: grey literature
source_hierarchy.definition: Research and reporting published outside commercial or academic channels.
source_hierarchy.example: Agency reports, think-tank studies, technical notes.
source_hierarchy.caution: Not indexed consistently; assess the producing body's method and interest directly.

source_hierarchy.name: government report
source_hierarchy.definition: An official publication of a public body, often carrying data unavailable elsewhere.
source_hierarchy.caution: Mandate shapes scope; read the methodological annex and the terms of reference.

source_hierarchy.name: advocacy organization report
source_hierarchy.definition: Research published by an organization with a declared position on the subject.
source_hierarchy.caution: Often first to a neglected topic and methodologically uneven; check the data appendix, not the executive summary.

source_hierarchy.name: industry analyst report
source_hierarchy.definition: Market or technology analysis produced commercially, frequently paywalled.
source_hierarchy.caution: Methods are usually undisclosed and clients are usually the subjects.

source_hierarchy.name: trade press
source_hierarchy.definition: Journalism written for practitioners of a specific industry.
source_hierarchy.caution: Closer to operational reality than general press, and closer to the industry's framing.

source_hierarchy.name: general press report
source_hierarchy.definition: Reporting for a lay audience by a newsroom with editing and correction practices.
source_hierarchy.caution: A pointer to sources, not a source; headline claims routinely outrun the article's own body.

source_hierarchy.name: press release
source_hierarchy.definition: An announcement issued by an interested party to shape coverage.
source_hierarchy.caution: Institutional press releases systematically overstate the underlying study; go to the paper.

source_hierarchy.name: self-published commentary
source_hierarchy.definition: Blogs, newsletters, and posts published without editorial gatekeeping.
source_hierarchy.caution: Can be expert and current, or unaccountable; judge by the argument and the shown work, and cite with dates.

source_hierarchy.name: collaboratively edited reference
source_hierarchy.definition: A wiki or similar work whose content is edited by an open community with revision history.
source_hierarchy.caution: Use the revision history and the cited references; never cite the page for a contested claim.

source_hierarchy.name: social media post
source_hierarchy.definition: A short public statement by an account, occasionally the primary record of an announcement.
source_hierarchy.caution: Verify account authenticity, archive it, and distinguish an official statement from a personal one.

source_hierarchy.name: binding legal authority
source_hierarchy.definition: A statute, regulation, or decision that controls the question within a jurisdiction.
source_hierarchy.caution: Check currency and jurisdiction; superseded law reads exactly like current law.

source_hierarchy.name: persuasive legal authority
source_hierarchy.definition: A decision or commentary that carries argumentative weight without binding force.
source_hierarchy.caution: Label it as persuasive; presenting it as controlling is a citation error with substantive consequences.

source_hierarchy.name: agency guidance
source_hierarchy.definition: An interpretive document explaining how a regulator reads its own rules.
source_hierarchy.caution: Usually not legally binding, frequently treated as if it were; note the distinction.

source_hierarchy.name: technical standard
source_hierarchy.definition: A published specification developed by a standards body, sometimes incorporated into law by reference.
source_hierarchy.caution: Versioned and often paywalled; cite the version and its date.

source_hierarchy.name: dataset with codebook
source_hierarchy.definition: Released data accompanied by variable definitions, collection method, and known limitations.
source_hierarchy.caution: Data without a codebook cannot be interpreted, only manipulated.

source_hierarchy.name: retracted publication
source_hierarchy.definition: A paper formally withdrawn by journal or authors for error or misconduct.
source_hierarchy.caution: Retracted work keeps accumulating citations for years; check retraction databases before citing anything old and load-bearing.
